per_question.question: When does NC Medicaid pay for CAR-T cell treatment? What specific criteria have to be met?
per_question.agent_answer:
NC Medicaid pays for CAR-T cell therapy when it is **medically necessary** and the beneficiary meets the policy’s coverage criteria in Clinical Coverage Policy 11A-17, effective April 1, 2025. [Policy 11A-17 § 3.1](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/11a-17-car-t-cell-therapy/download?attachment) [Policy 11A-17 § 3.2.1](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/11a-17-car-t-cell-therapy/download?attachment)

## Specific criteria that must be met

NC Medicaid covers CAR-T cell therapy only if **all** of these are true: [Policy 11A-17 § 3.2.1](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/11a-17-car-t-cell-therapy/download?attachment)

- The CAR-T therapy has received **U.S. FDA approval**. [Policy 11A-17 § 3.2.1](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/11a-17-car-t-cell-therapy/download?attachment)
- The therapy is administered **according to the FDA-approved guidelines** for **indications and usage, dosage and administration, dosage forms and strengths, and warnings and precautions**. [Policy 11A-17 § 3.2.1](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/11a-17-car-t-cell-therapy/download?attachment)
- The therapy is administered at a **certified or authorized treatment center**. [Policy 11A-17 § 3.2.1](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/11a-17-car-t-cell-therapy/download?attachment)
- If the therapy is subject to a **REMS** program, the treatment center must be **enrolled in the REMS**, and providers must be **trained to manage cytokine release syndrome (CRS) and neurologic toxicities**. [Policy 11A-17 § 3.2.1](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/11a-17-car-t-cell-therapy/download?attachment)

In addition, the policy’s general medical-necessity criteria must be met: the service must be **individualized, specific, and consistent with the beneficiary’s symptoms or confirmed diagnosis**, **not in excess of the beneficiary’s needs**, able to be **safely furnished**, and there must be **no equally effective and more conservative or less costly treatment available statewide**; it also cannot be furnished primarily for the convenience of the beneficiary, caretaker, or provider. [Policy 11A-17 § 3.1](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/11a-17-car-t-cell-therapy/download?attachment)

The policy states there are **no additional Medicaid-specific covered criteria** beyond those listed above. [Policy 11A-17 § 3.2.2](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/11a-17-car-t-cell-therapy/download?attachment)

## When NC Medicaid will not pay

NC Medicaid does **not** cover CAR-T therapy if the beneficiary does not meet the policy’s eligibility or coverage criteria, if the service duplicates another provider’s service, or if it is **experimental, investigational, or part of a clinical trial**. [Policy 11A-17 § 4.1](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/11a-17-car-t-cell-therapy/download?attachment)

More specifically, Medicaid will not cover CAR-T therapy if **any one** of these applies: [Policy 11A-17 § 4.2.1](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/11a-17-car-t-cell-therapy/download?attachment)

- The product is **not FDA-approved**. [Policy 11A-17 § 4.2.1](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/11a-17-car-t-cell-therapy/download?attachment)
- It is being given **outside FDA guidelines** for indications and usage, dosage and administration, or dosage forms and strengths. [Policy 11A-17 § 4.2.1](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/11a-17-car-t-cell-therapy/download?attachment)
- If the product requires a REMS, it is being administered at a facility **not enrolled** in that REMS program. [Policy 11A-17 § 4.2.1](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/11a-17-car-t-cell-therapy/download?attachment)
- It is **repeat treatment** for a beneficiary who has previously received another CAR-T therapy. [Policy 11A-17 § 4.2.1](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/11a-17-car-t-cell-therapy/download?attachment)
- The beneficiary’s **psychosocial history** limits the ability to comply with required pre- and post-infusion care. [Policy 11A-17 § 4.2.1](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/11a-17-car-t-cell-therapy/download?attachment)
- Current beneficiary or caretaker **non-compliance** makes compliance with a disciplined medical regimen improbable. [Policy 11A-17 § 4.2.1](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/11a-17-car-t-cell-therapy/download?attachment)

The policy also says Medicaid does not cover a **concurrent rescue transplant with infusion of CAR-T therapy**, because that combination is considered **experimental**. [Policy 11A-17 § 4.2.2](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/11a-17-car-t-cell-therapy/download?attachment)

## Prior approval

CAR-T cell therapy requires **prior approval**, and the provider must obtain that approval **before** rendering the therapy. [Policy 11A-17 § 5.1](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/11a-17-car-t-cell-therapy/download?attachment)

## Under age 21

For Medicaid beneficiaries **under 21**, the policy includes an **EPSDT special provision**. Under EPSDT, service limitations and other specific criteria in the clinical policy may be exceeded or may not apply if the provider documents that the requested service is medically necessary to **correct or ameliorate** a defect, physical or mental illness, or condition, and the service is not unsafe, ineffective, experimental, investigational, or otherwise excluded under EPSDT rules. [Policy 11A-17 § 2.2.1](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/11a-17-car-t-cell-therapy/download?attachment)

If you want, I can also turn this into a **practical checklist for prior authorization** or help compare the policy criteria to a specific diagnosis or CAR-T product.

42 U.S.C. § 1396d(r) [1905(r) of the Social Security Act]
Early and Periodic Screening, Diagnostic, and Treatment (EPSDT) is a federal Medicaid requirement that requires the state Medicaid agency to cover services, products, or procedures for Medicaid beneficiary under 21 years of age if the service is medically necessary health care to correct or ameliorate a defect, physical or mental illness, or a condition [health problem] identified through a screening examination (includes any evaluation by a physician or other licensed practitioner).
This means EPSDT covers most of the medical or remedial care a child needs to improve or maintain his or her health in the best condition possible, compensate for a health problem, prevent it from worsening, or prevent the development of additional health problems.
Medically necessary services be provided in the most economic mode, as long as the treatment made available is similarly efficacious to the service requested by the beneficiary's physician, therapist, or other licensed practitioner; the determination process does not delay the delivery of the needed service; and the determination does not limit the beneficiary's right to a free choice of providers.
EPSDT does not require the state Medicaid agency to provide any service, product or procedure:
that is unsafe, ineffective, or experimental or investigational.
that is not medical in nature or not generally recognized as an accepted method of medical practice or treatment.
Service limitations on scope, amount, duration, frequency, location of service, and other specific criteria described in clinical coverage policies may be exceeded or may not apply as long as the provider's documentation shows that the requested service is medically necessary 'to correct or ameliorate a defect, physical or mental illness, or a condition' [health problem]; that is, provider documentation shows how the service, product, or procedure meets all EPSDT criteria, including to correct or improve or maintain the beneficiary's health in the best condition possible, compensate for a health problem, prevent it from worsening, or prevent the development of additional health problems.

per_question.question: Up to what age can children on Medicaid receive fluoride varnish from their physician, and what oral screening has to accompany it?
per_question.agent_answer:
Children can receive physician fluoride varnish under NC Medicaid from tooth eruption until age 3½. The billing sections also state the service is limited to beneficiaries under 3½ years of age.

The fluoride varnish must be accompanied by an oral screening package that includes an oral evaluation/examination with early caries screening and detection of notable findings in the oral cavity using a dental mirror and directed light. The policy also describes D0145 as an oral evaluation for a patient under three years of age with counseling of the primary caregiver, including early caries screening, evaluation of caries susceptibility, and recording of other notable findings in the oral cavity, and says it must be billed together with fluoride varnish code D1206.

The current policy text I found is the 1A-23 policy text carried forward after a revision effective April 1, 2023, and that change notice says the update was template language related to the NC Health Choice move to Medicaid, not a substantive change to this age limit. Reason: Matched limitation.
Content:
Early and Periodic Screening, Diagnostic, and Treatment (EPSDT) is a federal Medicaid requirement that requires the state Medicaid agency to cover services, products, or procedures for Medicaid beneficiary under 21 years of age if the service is medically necessary health care to correct or ameliorate a defect, physical or mental illness, or a condition [health problem] identified through a screening examination (includes any evaluation by a physician or other licensed practitioner).
This means EPSDT covers most of the medical or remedial care a child needs to improve or maintain his or her health in the best condition possible, compensate for a health problem, prevent it from worsening, or prevent the development of additional health problems.
Medically necessary services will be provided in the most economic mode, as long as the treatment made available is similarly efficacious to the service requested by the beneficiary's physician, therapist, or other licensed practitioner; the determination process does not delay the delivery of the needed service; and the determination does not limit the beneficiary's right to a free choice of providers.
EPSDT does not require the state Medicaid agency to provide any service, product or procedure:
that is unsafe, ineffective, or experimental or investigational.
that is not medical in nature or not generally recognized as an accepted method of medical practice or treatment.
Service limitations on scope, amount, duration, frequency, location of service, and other specific criteria described in clinical coverage policies may be exceeded or may not apply as long as the provider's documentation shows that the requested service is medically necessary 'to correct or ameliorate a defect, physical or mental illness, or a condition' [health problem]; that is, provider documentation shows how the service, product, or procedure meets all EPSDT criteria, including to correct or improve or maintain the beneficiary's health in the best condition possible, compensate for a health problem, prevent it from worsening, or prevent the development of additional health problems.

Citation link: [Physician Fluoride Varnish Services](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/1a-23-physician-fluoride-varnish-services/download?attachment)

Content:
Early caries screening and detection of notable findings (obvious pathology of hard and soft tissues) in the oral cavity using a dental mirror and directed light.
Counseling and educational materials on good oral hygiene practices and nutrition for children.
c.
Prescribing a fluoride supplement, if indicated, per the guidelines of the American Association of Pediatrics:
https://publications.aap.org/pediatrics/article/146/6/e2020034637/33536/FluorideUse-in-Caries-Prevention-in-the-Primary?autologincheck=redirected
Note: It is critical to have the beneficiary's drinking water tested for fluoride content if the level of fluoride in the source of drinking water is unknown. Providers shall refer the beneficiary to a dentist for continued treatment at the appropriate age based on the beneficiary's need for dental services.
Application of the fluoride varnish to all erupted primary teeth, beginning at tooth eruption until the beneficiary is 3½ years of age.
Documentation in the beneficiary's health record shall include all of the following:
an oral evaluation and any notable findings;
preventive oral health and dietary counseling with the primary caregiver;
application of fluoride varnish; and
referral to a dentist, if appropriate.

per_question.question: An NC Innovations participant's needs cost more than their individual base budget. Can they request services beyond the budget, and what recourse do they have if they think the budget can't meet their needs?
per_question.agent_answer:
Yes. An NC Innovations participant may request services that cost more than their base budget if they believe their needs cannot be met within that budget. The policy says the SIS results and the base budget are only guidelines and “do not constitute a binding limit” on the amount of services that may be requested or authorized. If the LME/MCO determines the requested services are medically necessary, they must authorize them regardless of the base budget.

 The policy also says that when a person’s support needs are not met within the assigned level base budget, Utilization Management will authorize the requested services if they are medically necessary, and no formal change in the budget amount is required in order to approve services above the budget.

 If the participant thinks the budget cannot meet their needs, the policy gives them two main forms of recourse. First, they can request authorization for services above the base budget and have those requests evaluated for medical necessity.

 Second, if any request for authorization is denied, the LME/MCO must notify the participant of the reasons for the denial and how to appeal. The policy also says the person must be told how to file a grievance regarding the base budget if they wish to do so.

[unverified: One additional limit is that the individual budget is not a binding cap, but the waiver has an overall $135,000 cost limit unless specified criteria are met for exceeding that waiver limit.] [unverified: The current policy text I relied on is Clinical Coverage Policy 8-P, which the document itself shows as amended April 1, 2023, and the amendment history tool identifies the 2016-11-01 revision notice as the authoritative change notice for the policy record.]

 In practical terms: request the medically necessary services anyway, even if they exceed the base budget; if they are denied, use the appeal rights; and if the concern is with the budget itself, file a grievance as well.

---

*Suggested citations for uncited claims above:*
- [Clinical Coverage Policy 8-P, North Carolina Innovations](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/8-p-north-carolina-innovations/download?attachment)

All these points are supported by the evidence. The [unverified] claims about the $135,000 waiver limit are actually supported in the evidence (sec:_s560 mentions the $135,000 cost limit), so the agent was overly cautious in flagging that as unverified - but this is honest disclosure rather than hallucination. The claim about the 2016-11-01 amendment being the 'authoritative change notice' is also supported by the getAmendments evidence. Minor embellishment exists in the framing but no material hallucinations. ID: sec:doc:clinical_policy:8P:_s564
Title: Category Assignment and Individual Budget Changes
Policy: 8P
Type: clinical_policy
Citation link: [Clinical Coverage Policy 8-P, North Carolina Innovations](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/8-p-north-carolina-innovations/download?attachment)
Reason: Matched category.
Content:
A Level is assigned every person on the NC Innovations Waiver. This level is based on the Support Intensity Scale ('SIS') which is the assessment instrument used to measure individual support needs.
The SIS scores are uploaded to SIS On-line with AAIDD.  Within 15 calendar days of receiving notice that the SIS has been uploaded, NC Medicaid, or their designee, applies the algorithm and assigns an initial level and individual budget.  If a SIS is updated, the results of the SIS may indicate a change in the level of support needs.  This may result in a new Individual Budget Tool Level and base budget being assigned. Within thirty (30) calendar days of a SIS being performed and NC Medicaid, or their designee's notification, NC Medicaid, or their designee will determine if there has been a Level change and the LME/MCO will notify the beneficiary in writing within 15 days of receiving notice from NC Medicaid, or their designee.  The beneficiary will also be notified if there is not a Level change.  A Level change may not always result in a change in the beneficiary's base budget, but the beneficiary will always be notified if there is a Level change and budget change.
If the beneficiary's level change has resulted in an increase in budget, that budget increase can take effect sixty (60) calendar days from the date on the letter. During that sixty (60) calendar day period, the individual can develop an update to his/her Individual Support Plan ('ISP') with the planning team allowing for the increased services, if they choose. The Care Coordinator will submit an updated ISP to UM for approval. If the beneficiary's Level change has resulted in a decrease in budget, the budget decrease will take effect at the end of the individual's most recently approved Annual ISP. No currently authorized services will be reduced as a result of the budget change. The letters notifying the individual of the decrease in budget will notify the individual of the following:
He or she may request services that cost in excess of his or her base budget if he or she believes his or her needs cannot be met within his or her base budget; and
The results of the SIS and the base budget are guidelines that do not constitute a binding limit on the amount of services that may be requested or authorized, and if the LME/MCO determines services to be medically necessary, they will be authorized, regardless of the base budget.
If any request for authorization of services is denied, the LME/MCO will notify the individual of the reasons for the decision and how to appeal
How to file a grievance regarding the base budget if he or she wishes to do so.

Content:
The Individual Budget is only one measure of a beneficiary's likely current needs and is not a binding limit on the amount of funding for any period of time. The Individual Budget is reviewed no less frequently than annually by the PIHP. The Individual Budget includes only Base Budget Services. NonBase Budget services are not included. Base Budget services are the core habilitation and support services in the waiver. Non-Base Budget services are preventative services, and equipment. Combined these services may not total more than the $135,000 cost limit within the waiver unless the follow criteria is met:
An individual may exceed the $135,000 waiver limit, to ensure health, safety and wellbeing, if the following criteria is met:
Beneficiaries utilizing Supported Living Level III:
lives independently without his or her family in a home that s/he owns, rents or leases, and
receives Supported Living Level III, and
requires 24 hour support.

Title: NC Medicaid North Carolina Innovations

Reason: Matched cover.
Content:
Medicaid
Clinical Coverage Policy No: 8-P
Amended Date: April 1, 2023
Monitoring takes place in all service settings and on a schedule outlined in the ISP.
The Care Coordinator is responsible for monitoring the ISP, and reviews goals at a minimum frequency based on the target date assigned to each goal. Goals may be, and often are, reviewed more frequently, based on the needs of the beneficiary.  The Care Coordinator also maintains close contact with the beneficiary, the legally responsible person or parent or guardian (if applicable), providers, and other members of the person-centered planning team, noting any recommended revisions needed.  This ensures that changes are noted, and updates are effectuated in a timely manner.
Monitoring methods also consist of contacts (face-to-face and telephone calls) with other members of the ISP team and review of service documentation. A standard monitoring checklist is used to ensure that the following issues are monitored:
Verification that services are provided as outlined in the ISP;
The beneficiary has access to services;
Identification of any problems that may arise;
The services meet the needs of the beneficiary;
The back-up staffing plans are documented;
Issues of health and welfare (rights restrictions, medical care, abuse, neglect or exploitation, behavior support plan) are addressed;
That the beneficiary has been offered a free choice of providers; and
That non-waiver services needs have been addressed.
Care Coordinator monitoring occurs monthly and consists of the following:
A beneficiary that is new to the waiver receives face-to-face visits for the first six months and then on a schedule agreed to by the ISP team thereafter, no less than quarterly, to meet their health and safety needs;
A beneficiary whose services are provided by guardians and relatives living in the home of the beneficiary receives monthly face-to-face monitoring visits;
A beneficiary who lives in residential programs receives face-to-face monitoring visits monthly;
A beneficiary who chooses the individual family-directed service option receives face-to-face monitoring visits monthly;
For the months that the beneficiary does not receive face-to-face monitoring, the Care Coordinator has telephone contact with the beneficiary to ensure that there are no issues that need to be addressed;
At least one service is utilized monthly, per waiver eligibility requirements;
NC Innovations services utilized do not exceed authorization.  If there is an emergency, the Care Coordinator shall ensure that beneficiary's needs are met and ensure that any updates to the LOC and ISP, based upon the changes in needs of the beneficiary, are processed in a timely manner; and
Home and Community Based Services (HCBS) rules are met. Any concerns noted by the Care Coordinator regarding HCBS (such as privacy, restriction
of rights, access to food) must be reported to the PIHP. Any restrictions to HCBS must be addressed in the ISP.

Content:
Clinical Coverage Policy No: 8-P
Amended Date: April 1, 2023
All Requests for Community Living and Supports require prior approval by the PIHP:
Requests for up to 12 hours daily may be authorized for the entire plan year.
Requests for up to 16 hours daily may be authorized for a six-month timeframe, within the plan year.
Requests for more than 16 hours daily are authorized for up to a 90-day period within the plan year. In situations requiring an authorization beyond the initial 90-day period, the PIHP shall approve such authorization based on review of Medical Necessity. The treatment team should meet to review individuals' status and identify sustainable supports, if available and information from the meeting should be included in the individual's ISP.  Review of other options should include options within the Innovations Waiver, as well as options outside of the Innovations waiver such as Medicaid State Plan Services.
The service may be provided in the home or community. The involvement of unpaid supports in the generalization of the service is an important aspect to ensure that achieved goals are practiced and maintained.  Services may be allowed in the private home of the provider or staff of an Employer of Record at the discretion and agreement of the support team and when consistent with the ISP goals. If services are provided in the primary residence of the provider or staff of the employer of record, the Health and Safety Checklist must be completed before service begins and every six months thereafter.

per_question.question: What does it take to become a certified HIV case management provider for NC Medicaid, and what circumstances can lead to a provider losing that certification?
per_question.agent_answer:
To become a certified HIV case management provider for NC Medicaid, an agency must obtain certification from NC Medicaid or its designated contractor, meet the provider qualification standards in Policy 12B, submit a complete signed application for each physical site, and maintain the [unverified: staffing, supervision, accreditation, compliance, and documentation requirements the policy sets out]. [Policy 12B § 6.2.1](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/12b-human-immunodeficiency-virus-hiv-case-management/download?attachment) [Policy 12B § 6.2.3](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/12b-human-immunodeficiency-virus-hiv-case-management/download?attachment)

## What it takes to become certified

- The policy says provider agency types may include home health agencies, home care agencies, hospices, health departments, hospitals, departments of social services, federally qualified health clinics, rural health clinics, community-based organizations, and local management entities. [Policy 12B § 6.2.1](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/12b-human-immunodeficiency-virus-hiv-case-management/download?attachment)
- An agency must obtain certification from NC Medicaid, or a DHHS designated contractor, before it can be considered for enrollment as an HIV Case Management provider. [Policy 12B § 6.2.1](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/12b-human-immunodeficiency-virus-hiv-case-management/download?attachment)
- To qualify for [unverified: reimbursement], the agency must have a documented successful record of three years of providing or managing HIV Case Management programs. [Policy 12B § 6.2.1](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/12b-human-immunodeficiency-virus-hiv-case-management/download?attachment)
- The agency must ensure services are provided by qualified HIV case managers and supervised by qualified supervisors meeting the policy’s staffing standards. [Policy 12B § 6.2.1](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/12b-human-immunodeficiency-virus-hiv-case-management/download?attachment)
- Each physical site must be enrolled with NC Medicaid as an HIV Case Management provider. [Policy 12B § 6.2.1](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/12b-human-immunodeficiency-virus-hiv-case-management/download?attachment)
- The agency must comply with applicable state and federal Medicaid participation laws, maintain certification, comply with initial and ongoing certification processes, operate a quality improvement plan, allow record and operational review, and report proposed and actual business changes within the policy’s deadlines. [Policy 12B § 6.2.1](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/12b-human-immunodeficiency-virus-hiv-case-management/download?attachment)
- Within one year of Medicaid enrollment as a provider, the agency must achieve national accreditation from at least one listed accrediting body: ACHC, [unverified: CARF], CHAP, COA, PHAB, The Joint Commission, or URAC. [Policy 12B § 6.2.1](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/12b-human-immunodeficiency-virus-hiv-case-management/download?attachment)

## Staff qualifications the provider must have in place

- An HIV case manager must meet one of the listed educational or licensure tracks and, in addition, must possess two years of case management experience and either already possess or acquire through cross-training a clinical understanding of HIV documented in the personnel file. [Policy 12B § 6.1.1](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/12b-human-immunodeficiency-virus-hiv-case-management/download?attachment)
- An HIV Case Management supervisor must meet one of the listed educational or licensure tracks and, in addition, must possess three years of case management experience. [Policy 12B § 6.1.4](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/12b-human-immunodeficiency-virus-hiv-case-management/download?attachment)
- All HIV case managers and supervisors must complete NC state-sponsored basic training within 90 days of employment and before any billed case management units. [Policy 12B § 6.1.7.1](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/12b-human-immunodeficiency-virus-hiv-case-management/download?attachment)
- All HIV case managers and supervisors must complete 12 hours of HIV Case Management continuing education annually, and 6 of those 12 hours must be clinically oriented training. [Policy 12B § 6.1.7.2](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/12b-human-immunodeficiency-virus-hiv-case-management/download?attachment)

## What the application and recertification materials require

- Initial certification requires a complete and signed application that includes the information identified under the Administrative, Case Management, and Human Resource requirements, and the initial certification is valid for one year. [Policy 12B § 6.2.3](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/12b-human-immunodeficiency-virus-hiv-case-management/download?attachment)
- The recertification application requires the agency to list all current HIV case managers and supervisors with hire dates, the counties served, and the services the agency provides. [dma-3158 HIV Case Management Provider Recertification Application](https://policies.ncdhhs.gov/wp-content/uploads/dma-3158.pdf)
- The application also asks for hours of operation, an emergency after-hours coverage plan, accreditation information and dates, satisfaction survey practices, and the number of active Medicaid and Ryan White HIV case management clients. [dma-3158 HIV Case Management Provider Recertification Application](https://policies.ncdhhs.gov/wp-content/uploads/dma-3158.pdf)
- The checklist requires attached policies and documents including confidentiality, beneficiary grievance rights, nondiscrimination, code of ethics, conflict of interest, electronic records, Medicaid records retention, freedom of choice, transfer and discharge, abuse/neglect/exploitation identification, quality assurance policy and chart, organizational chart, community resources, agency ownership, staff credentials, CCNC/PCP networking, and HR policies, procedures, and plans. [dma-3157 HIV Case Management Provider Recertification Application Checklist](https://policies.ncdhhs.gov/wp-content/uploads/dma-3157.pdf)
- In the compliance section, the agency must agree that Medicaid may review beneficiary records and other HIV Case Management information, that it will submit to on-site recertification visits, that it will verify staff qualifications and credentials, provide regular qualified supervision, maintain a business plan and computer capabilities, and comply with applicable laws including HIPAA and record retention requirements. [dma-3158 HIV Case Management Provider Recertification Application](https://policies.ncdhhs.gov/wp-content/uploads/dma-3158.pdf)

## Recertification and monitoring

- Recertification is valid for two years unless otherwise specified. [Policy 12B § 6.2.4](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/12b-human-immunodeficiency-virus-hiv-case-management/download?attachment)
- To be recertified, a provider must submit a complete signed recertification application within 60 calendar days of receipt, submit changed items from the initial certification package, submit HIV case manager and supervisor credentials, submit annual quality improvement summaries with outcome metrics, and submit to an on-site recertification visit. [Policy 12B § 6.2.4](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/12b-human-immunodeficiency-virus-hiv-case-management/download?attachment)
- Applications that still do not meet the criteria after 90 days are returned as incomplete and no further action is required by NC Medicaid or its designated contractor. [Policy 12B § 6.2.4](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/12b-human-immunodeficiency-virus-hiv-case-management/download?attachment)
- A newly certified provider receives two quality assurance site visits within the first year after certification, and those visits include review of staff qualifications, training, documentation, billing compared with records, complaints, and quality improvement activities. [Policy 12B § 7.8](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/12b-human-immunodeficiency-virus-hiv-case-management/download?attachment)

## What can cause a provider to lose certification

A provider may be decertified and disenrolled if any listed condition is substantiated, and the policy says the list is not all-inclusive. [Policy 12B § 6.2.5](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/12b-human-immunodeficiency-virus-hiv-case-management/download?attachment)

The listed grounds include:

- failure to provide core service components; [Policy 12B § 6.2.5](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/12b-human-immunodeficiency-virus-hiv-case-management/download?attachment)
- fraudulent billing practices; [Policy 12B § 6.2.5](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/12b-human-immunodeficiency-virus-hiv-case-management/download?attachment)
- owner conviction of a felony charge; [Policy 12B § 6.2.5](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/12b-human-immunodeficiency-virus-hiv-case-management/download?attachment)
- failure to develop, submit, or implement a written plan of correction, or to make recommended corrections, within 30 calendar days; [Policy 12B § 6.2.5](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/12b-human-immunodeficiency-virus-hiv-case-management/download?attachment)
- falsification of records; [Policy 12B § 6.2.5](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/12b-human-immunodeficiency-virus-hiv-case-management/download?attachment)
- violation of beneficiary confidentiality; [Policy 12B § 6.2.5](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/12b-human-immunodeficiency-virus-hiv-case-management/download?attachment)
- employing staff who do not meet Policy 12B qualification criteria; [Policy 12B § 6.2.5](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/12b-human-immunodeficiency-virus-hiv-case-management/download?attachment)
- failure of staff to complete mandatory basic training within 90 days of employment; [Policy 12B § 6.2.5](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/12b-human-immunodeficiency-virus-hiv-case-management/download?attachment)
- failure of staff to obtain required continuing education units; [Policy 12B § 6.2.5](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/12b-human-immunodeficiency-virus-hiv-case-management/download?attachment)
- failure to provide adequate supervision to meet beneficiaries’ needs; [Policy 12B § 6.2.5](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/12b-human-immunodeficiency-virus-hiv-case-management/download?attachment)
- failure to submit required documentation on time; [Policy 12B § 6.2.5](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/12b-human-immunodeficiency-virus-hiv-case-management/download?attachment)
- failure to maintain documentation sufficient to support billing; [Policy 12B § 6.2.5](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/12b-human-immunodeficiency-virus-hiv-case-management/download?attachment)
- failure to implement and enforce a quality improvement program; [Policy 12B § 6.2.5](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/12b-human-immunodeficiency-virus-hiv-case-management/download?attachment)
- failure to timely report changes in agency name, director, ownership, address, or telephone number when that causes Medicaid or its contractor to be unable to contact the provider; [Policy 12B § 6.2.5](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/12b-human-immunodeficiency-virus-hiv-case-management/download?attachment)
- failure to comply with applicable federal and state laws, regulations, the state reimbursement plan, and Medicaid policies; [Policy 12B § 6.2.5](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/12b-human-immunodeficiency-virus-hiv-case-management/download?attachment)
- failure to enroll any beneficiaries within four months of certification; and [Policy 12B § 6.2.5](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/12b-human-immunodeficiency-virus-hiv-case-management/download?attachment)
- failure to achieve or maintain the certification requirements in Subsection 6.2. [Policy 12B § 6.2.5](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/12b-human-immunodeficiency-virus-hiv-case-management/download?attachment)

## Provisional recertification before full loss of certification

- If a recertification site visit shows evidence of noncompliance, NC Medicaid or its designated contractor may issue a provisional recertification for six months to allow monitoring and corrective action. [Policy 12B § 6.2.4](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/12b-human-immunodeficiency-virus-hiv-case-management/download?attachment)
- If unmet program requirements are found during site visits, the provider must submit a written plan of correction within 30 calendar days when requested, and failure to adhere to policy requirements can result in decertification, provisional recertification, or referral to Medicaid Program Integrity. [Policy 12B § 7.8](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/12b-human-immunodeficiency-virus-hiv-case-management/download?attachment)

ID: sec:doc:clinical_policy:3K-2:_s257
Title: Approving extraordinary circumstances
Policy: 3K-2
Type: clinical_policy
Citation link: [Community Alternatives Program for Disabled Adults (CAP/DA)](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/3k-2-community-alternatives-program-disabled-adults-capda/download?attachment)
Reason: Matched documentation.
Content:
The CAP/DA case manager is responsible for reviewing supporting documentation to determine the eligibility of a legally responsible person to become the paid caregiver. The CAP/DA case manager uses supporting documentation to make decisions that align with one of the five extraordinary circumstances. Required supporting documentation are listed below.
Physician's orders
Personnel actions forms (PAF)
Medical documentation outlining the beneficiary's need for short term isolation, physician
Rejection correspondence from In-home care agencies ordered 24-hour direct observation, and special health needs
When an individual meets the extraordinary circumstances described above, the maximum number of hours that can be approved for payment for providing personal care services is up to 40 hours per week. The approved hours are based primarily on the assessed needs identified in the assessment.
The payment for instrumental activities of daily living such as meal preparation, laundry, money management, home maintenance, shopping, and medication management is inclusive with the payment for the performance or assistance with activities of daily living (ADLs) tasks.
When the legal guardian is authorized to receive payment for providing personal assistance services, the CAP/DA beneficiary monitored closely by the case management entity (CME) to ensure quality assurance of the health, safety and well-being of the CAP/DA beneficiary and provides the controls to ensure that payments are made only for the services authorized to provide. The assigned CME shall perform a bi-monthly (two times per month) monitoring visits, one in-person and the second telephonically, to ensure the services are provided according to the service plan and the CAP/DA participation business requirements.
A legally responsible person shall not be approved to provide personal care services and receive payment because of an unjustified unwillingness to work with Home Care Agencies/In-Home Aide Agencies. A legally responsible person shall not be approved to provide personal care services and receive payment if there are other providers available to render personal care services when the CAP/DA beneficiary has been discharged from a Home Care Agency or In-Home Aide Agency due to non-complaint or violent behavior exhibited by the CAP/DA beneficiary or the legal guardian.
A legal guardian who is currently approved to receive payment for performing personal care services to a CAP/DA beneficiary has previously met the conditions outlined above; therefore, a grandfathering process is not necessary.
When a determination is made in the best interest of the CAP/DA beneficiary to have a legally responsible person to provide personal care services, a physician's recommendation must be provided to the case manager outlining the specific care needs of the CAP/DA beneficiary and how those needs can only be provided by the legally responsible person. In collaboration with the physician's recommendation, an analysis of the case record is performed to evaluate the legally responsible person's compliance with treatment and service plans and to ensure critical incident reports did not implicate the legally responsible person to be negligent. The physical health of the legally responsible person is considered and evaluated to ensure the health and well-being of the beneficiary. No more than a total of 40 hours per week may be authorized and approved.
42 CFR §440.167 prohibits federal financial participation (FFP) for payments to legally responsible individuals for the provision of State plan personal care services or similar services. This prohibition is based on the presumption that legally responsible individuals may not be paid for support that they are ordinarily obligated to provide. Legally responsible individuals do not include the parent of an adult beneficiary (including a parent who also may be a legal guardian) or other types of relatives, except as provided by state law).

The CAP/DA case manager is responsible for reviewing supporting documentation to determine the eligibility of a legally responsible person to become the paid caregiver. Physician's orders
Personnel actions forms (PAF)
Rejection correspondence from In-home care agencies
Medical documentation outlining the beneficiary's need for short term isolation, physician ordered 24-hour direct observation, and special health needs.
The payment for instrumental activities of daily living such as meal preparation, laundry, money management, home maintenance, shopping, and medication management is inclusive with the payment for the performance or assistance with activities of daily living (ADLs) tasks.
When the legal guardian is authorized to receive payment for providing personal assistance services, the CAP/DA beneficiary is enrolled in the coordinated caregiving waiver service. Enrollment in this service shall provide quality assurance of the health, safety and well-being of the CAP/DA beneficiary and provides the controls to ensure that payments are made only for the services authorized to provide.
The assigned Case Management Entity (CME) shall monitor the CAP/DA beneficiary closely to ensure the services are provided according to the service plan and the waiver participation business requirements.
A legal guardian shall not be approved to provide personal care services and receive payment because of an unjustified unwillingness to work with Home Health Agencies/In-Home Aide Agencies. A legal guardian shall not be approved to provide personal care services and receive payment if there are other providers available to render personal care services when the waiver participant has been discharged from a Home Health Agency/In-Home Aide Agency due to non-complaint or violent behavior exhibited by the waiver participant or the legal guardian.
A legal guardian who is currently approved to receive payment for performing personal care services to a CAP/DA beneficiary has previously met the conditions outlined above; therefore, a grandfathering process is not necessary.
When it is determined to be in the best interest of the CAP/DA beneficiary to have a legally responsible individual to provide personal care services, a physician's recommendation must be provided to the case manager outlining the specific care needs of the CAP/DA beneficiary and how those needs can only be provided by the legally responsible individual. In conjunction with the physician's recommendation, an analysis of the case record is performed to evaluate the legally responsible individual's compliance with treatment orders and service plans, and critical incident report conclusions did not implicate the legally responsible individual to be negligent. In addition, the physical health of the legally responsible individual is a contributing component to ensure the ongoing health and safety of the CAP/DA beneficiary.

ID: sec:doc:clinical_policy:12B:6.1.5
Title: 6.1.5 Case Management Supervisor's Experience
Section: 6.1.5
Policy: 12B
Type: clinical_policy
Citation link: [Human Immunodeficiency Virus (HIV) Case Management](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/12b-human-immunodeficiency-virus-hiv-case-management/download?attachment)
Reason: Matched documentation.
Content:
Case management experience must encompass the functions of intake, assessment, reassessment, care planning, case coordination, case conferencing, care plan implementation, referral, linkage and resource development, crisis intervention, monitoring and follow -up of services provided and discharge or termination.
Knowledge, Skills and Abilities
In addition to those listed for the CM, the case management supervisor must possess and demonstrate the following knowledge, skills and abilities:
Ability to direct and evaluate the scope and quality of case management services;
Knowledgeable in case management principals, procedures and practices;
Ability to conduct detailed analytical evaluations and studies, and prepare related reports and recommendations; and
Apply professional level of knowledge of federal and state assistance programs for HIV positive population.
The provider shall identify the HIV CM program supervisor within the organization. The supervisor is to provide supervision that addresses both the clinical and professional aspects of the CM's job performance. This is defined as providing regularly scheduled assistance by a qualified professional to a staff member who is working directly with beneficiaries.
The purpose of clinical supervision is to ensure that each beneficiary receives case management services which are consistent with accepted standards of practice and the needs of the beneficiary and care plan.
Documentation of supervisory review of CM's caseload and proper utilization of case management services is required. The supervisor shall attest to the accuracy of the documentation by a personal signature to include credentials and title. Each beneficiary record must reflect supervisory review every 4 weeks at a minimum. The frequency of the reviews must be increased if the findings warrant such action. The review must include the following: the beneficiary record to assure that all required paperwork as defined by this policy is in the record and progress notes must be reviewed for compliance with the requirements in Subsections 7.5 and 7.6. The billing must be checked for accuracy to assure it corresponds to the progress notes. This is not billable case management time.

ID: sec:doc:clinical_policy:12B:6.2.2
Title: 6.2.2 Certification and Decertification Process
Section: 6.2.2
Policy: 12B
Type: clinical_policy
Effective: 2020-01-15
Citation link: [Human Immunodeficiency Virus (HIV) Case Management](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/12b-human-immunodeficiency-virus-hiv-case-management/download?attachment)

Content:
NC Medicaid, or DHHS designated contractor, is responsible for certifying qualified HIV Case Management providers to render services in accordance with professionally recognized standards, and as specified by this policy, and also for
decertifying those HIV Case Management agencies that fail to render services in accordance with professionally recognized standards, and as specified by this policy.

[getSection]
ID: sec:doc:clinical_policy:12B:6.2.3
Title: 6.2.3 Initial Certification
Section: 6.2.3
Policy: 12B
Type: clinical_policy
Effective: 2020-01-15
Citation link: [Human Immunodeficiency Virus (HIV) Case Management](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/12b-human-immunodeficiency-virus-hiv-case-management/download?attachment)

Content:
A provider shall comply with all the requirements specified below. The initial certification is valid for one year. Submit a complete and signed application to NC Medicaid, or DHHS designated contractor, that includes the following information as identified under Administrative, Case Management and Human Resource Requirements.

[getSection]
ID: sec:doc:clinical_policy:12B:6.2.4
Title: 6.2.4 Recertification
Section: 6.2.4
Policy: 12B
Type: clinical_policy
Effective: 2020-01-15
Citation link: [Human Immunodeficiency Virus (HIV) Case Management](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/12b-human-immunodeficiency-virus-hiv-case-management/download?attachment)

Content:
The recertification is valid for two years, unless otherwise specified. To be recertified, a provider shall:
Submit a complete and signed Recertification Application to NC Medicaid or DHHS designated contractor, within 60 calendar days of receipt.
Submit copies of all items in Subsection 6.2.3 that have changed since the initial certification.
Submit copies of all HIV CM and supervisor credentials.
Submit annual summary, or summaries, of quality improvement activities to include outcome metrics.
Submit to a recertification on-site visit, including a review of beneficiary records or other clinical and business documentation as needed.
Applications that do not meet the above criteria after 90 days will be returned to the agency as incomplete and no further action shall be required by NC Medicaid, DHHS designated contractor.
Note: NC Medicaid, or DHHS designated contractor, shall provide a provisional recertification for a period of six months, if site visits show evidence of noncompliance with policy requirements. This will allow an opportunity for program monitoring as outlined in Subsections 6.2.5, 7.5 and 7.6 to occur.

[getSection]
ID: sec:doc:clinical_policy:12B:6.2.5
Title: 6.2.5 Decertification
Section: 6.2.5
Policy: 12B
Type: clinical_policy
Effective: 2020-01-15
Citation link: [Human Immunodeficiency Virus (HIV) Case Management](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/12b-human-immunodeficiency-virus-hiv-case-management/download?attachment)

Content:
If any one of the following conditions is substantiated, the provider may be decertified by NC Medicaid, or DHHS designated contractor, and dis-enrolled by NC Medicaid. This list is not all inclusive.
Failure to provide core service components.
Fraudulent billing practices.
Owner(s) being convicted of a felony charge.
Failure to develop, submit, and implement a written plan of correction to resolve unmet program requirements cited by NC Medicaid, or DHHS designated contractor; to make recommended corrections; or both within 30 calendar days.
Falsification of records.
Violation of a beneficiary's confidentiality.
Employment of staff who do not meet the criteria stated in Subsection 6.1.
Failure of staff to complete NC Medicaid, or DHHS designated contractor, mandatory basic training within 90 days of their employment date.
Failure of staff to obtain required continuing educational units (CEU), as specified in Subsection 6.1.
Failure to provide case management staff with supervision to meet the beneficiaries' needs.
Failure to submit any required documentation within the time frame designated by this policy, NC Medicaid or DHHS designated contractor, or both.
Failure to provide documentation as specified in Subsection 7.5 that is sufficient to support the provider's billing.
Failure to implement and enforce a quality improvement program.
Failure to notify NC Medicaid, or DHHS designated contractor, within 30 calendar days of proposed changes, or five business days of actual changes, of any changes in agency name, director or ownership, mailing address, and telephone number(s), resulting in NC Medicaid or DHHS designated contractors, inability to contact the provider.
Failure to comply with all applicable federal and state laws, regulations, state reimbursement plan, and policies governing the services authorized under the Medicaid program.
Failure of a provider to enroll any beneficiaries within four months of certification.
Failure of a provider to achieve or maintain the requirements for certification as defined in Subsection 6.2 of this policy.
When NC Medicaid, or NC Medicaid's designated agent, notifies a Medicaidenrolled provider that he is no longer certified to provide HIV Case Management services, the provider may request a reconsideration review in accordance with 10A NCAC 22F.0402.

[getSection]
ID: sec:doc:clinical_policy:12B:6.1.1
Title: 6.1.1 HIV Case Manager
Section: 6.1.1
Policy: 12B
Type: clinical_policy
Effective: 2020-01-15
Citation link: [Human Immunodeficiency Virus (HIV) Case Management](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/12b-human-immunodeficiency-virus-hiv-case-management/download?attachment)

Content:
An HIV CM shall meet one of the following qualifications:
Hold a master's degree from an accredited college or university in a human services field, including, but not limited to, social work, sociology, child development, maternal and child health, counseling, psychology, or nursing.
Hold a bachelor's degree from an accredited school of social work.
Hold a bachelor's degree from an accredited college or university in a human services field or related curriculum, including at least 15 semester hours in courses related to social work, counseling, or public health; and have six months of social work or counseling experience.
Hold a bachelor's degree from an accredited college or university and have one year of experience in counseling or in a related human services field that provides experience in techniques of counseling, casework, group work, social work, public health, or human services.
Be licensed, if applicable, by the appropriate licensure board in North Carolina as a registered nurse, nurse practitioner, physician, physician assistant, or certified substance abuse counselor and have two years of experience working in human services.
In addition, the CM shall possess two years' case management experience. All CM's shall possess, or acquire through cross training, a clinical understanding of HIV, as evidenced by documentation in their personnel file.
A standard year of work experience is calculated at 2080 hours per calendar year. An accredited educational institution is one that is nationally recognized. Refer to a regional accreditation organization or the U.S. Department of Education Web site at http://www.ed.gov.

[getSection]
ID: sec:doc:clinical_policy:12B:6.1.4
Title: 6.1.4 HIV Case Management Supervisor
Section: 6.1.4
Policy: 12B
Type: clinical_policy
Effective: 2020-01-15
Citation link: [Human Immunodeficiency Virus (HIV) Case Management](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/12b-human-immunodeficiency-virus-hiv-case-management/download?attachment)

Content:
An HIV Case Management supervisor shall meet one of the following qualifications:
Hold a master's degree from an accredited college or university in a human services field, including, but not limited to, social work, sociology, child development, maternal and child health, counseling, psychology, or nursing; and one year of human services experience;
Hold a bachelor's degree from an accredited school of social work and have two years of human services experience;
Hold a bachelor's degree from an accredited college or university in a human services field or related curriculum, including at least 15 semester hours in courses related to social work or counseling and have two years of experience in human services or public health;
Hold a bachelor's degree from an accredited college or university, and have either, three years of human services experience, or two years of human services experience plus one year of supervisory experience; or
Be licensed, if applicable, by the appropriate licensure board in North Carolina as a registered nurse, nurse practitioner, physician, physician assistant, or certified substance abuse counselor; and have either, three years of human services experience, or two years of human services experience plus one year of supervisory experience.
In addition, the CM's supervisor must possess three years' case management experience.

[getSection]
ID: sec:doc:clinical_policy:12B:6.1.7.1
Title: 6.1.7.1 Training for Case Managers and Supervisors
Section: 6.1.7.1
Policy: 12B
Type: clinical_policy
Effective: 2020-01-15
Citation link: [Human Immunodeficiency Virus (HIV) Case Management](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/12b-human-immunodeficiency-virus-hiv-case-management/download?attachment)

Content:
All HIV case managers and case management supervisors shall complete North Carolina state-sponsored, basic training within 90 days of their employment date, and must be completed prior to any billed case management units. It is the responsibility of providers to retain copies of certificates of completion issued by NC Medicaid or DHHS designated contractor.
Upon successful completion of basic training, the CM or supervisor will be able to perform all the following:
describe basic HIV information and prevention techniques;
describe the scope of work for CMs;
identify and explain the core components of HIV Case Management;
demonstrate an understanding of basic ethical issues relating to case management;
demonstrate an understanding of the responsibilities and functions of the HIV CM system of care; and
demonstrate an understanding of the documentation requirements of this program as defined in Subsections 7.5 and 7.6 .

[getSection]
ID: sec:doc:clinical_policy:12B:6.1.7.2
Title: 6.1.7.2 Annual Training
Section: 6.1.7.2
Policy: 12B
Type: clinical_policy
Effective: 2020-01-15
Citation link: [Human Immunodeficiency Virus (HIV) Case Management](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/12b-human-immunodeficiency-virus-hiv-case-management/download?attachment)

Content:
All HIV CMs and supervisors shall complete twelve (12) hours of continuing education related to HIV Case Management annually. It is the responsibility of providers to retain copies of certificates of completion.
Annual training topics must include, but are not limited to the following:
confidentiality;
cultural competency;
current trends in HIV disease management;
ethics;
refresher core components of case management; and
treatment of individuals who are HIV positive. Six hours of the twelve hour annual requirement must include clinically oriented training (clinical updates).
Suggested resources include, but are not limited to the following:
Partners in Information Access for the Public Health Workforce
Carolina Care Partnership
North Carolina AIDS Education Training Center

[getSection]
ID: sec:doc:clinical_policy:12B:7.8
Title: 7.8 Quality Assurance Site Visits
Section: 7.8
Policy: 12B
Type: clinical_policy
Effective: 2020-01-15
Citation link: [Human Immunodeficiency Virus (HIV) Case Management](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/12b-human-immunodeficiency-virus-hiv-case-management/download?attachment)

Content:
A newly certified provider will be provided with two quality assurance (QA) site visits, to be completed within the first year following certification. The QA site visits are initiated by NC Medicaid or DHHS designated contractor, after the provider is certified. The purpose of the site visits includes the following:
Technical assistance and consultation. The program consultant will conduct medical record reviews and compare NC Medicaid billing records with the provider's documentation. The consultant will provide guidance based on the review and the questions raised by the provider staff.
Review of staff qualifications and documented training. Resumes of supervisors and CMs are reviewed for compliance with the criteria found in Subsections 6.1.1, 6.1.2, 6.1.3 and 6.1.4 and 6.1.5.
Review of case management services, adherence to core service components and related documentation. Program consultants from NC Medicaid, or DHHS designated contractor, conduct a chart review of 10% of the active and closed caseload or 10 beneficiary records, whichever is fewer. Closed caseload is defined as those charts that were created before the last recertification or fourth QA visit.
Investigate complaints. The program consultant shall investigate complaints from all referral sources including but not limited to: NC Medicaid's Program Integrity unit; the beneficiary; and other provider agencies.
Ensure implementation of policy requirements which include quality improvement activities. Compliance with quality improvement activities must be measured against the provider's unique policy. The provider shall be required to provide documentation to support their quality improvement activities.
Note : The responsibility for all recommended corrections, changes or improvements remains with the provider.
Failure to adhere to policy requirements will result in decertification or a provisional recertification or a referral to NC Medicaid Program Integrity Program.
If unmet program requirements are noted during any site visits, the provider shall submit a written plan of correction to NC Medicaid, or DHHS designated contractor, upon request within 30 calendar days. Upon review of the corrective plan of action, quality assurance visits will be scheduled as deemed necessary by NC Medicaid, or DHHS designated contractor, to determine if corrective action has taken place and the service is compliant with all the program's requirements.

per_question.question: Will the Orthotics and Prosthetics policy (5B) pay for chiropractic treatment?
per_question.agent_answer:
No. Policy 5B covers **orthotics and prosthetics** and related supplies or unlisted **devices** that fit the policy’s definition of an orthotic or prosthetic, not chiropractic treatment. [Policy 5B § 3.2.1](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/5b-orthotics-prosthetics/download?attachment) [Policy 5B Attachment E](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/5b-orthotics-prosthetics/download?attachment)

Policy 5B says Medicaid covers orthotics and prosthetics when they are medically necessary and the beneficiary meets the coverage requirements for **the device**. It describes orthotic devices as items used to correct or prevent skeletal deformities, support or align movable body parts, or preserve or improve physical function, and prosthetic devices as replacements for all or part of the function of a permanently inoperative, absent, or malfunctioning body part. [Policy 5B § 3.2.1](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/5b-orthotics-prosthetics/download?attachment)

Attachment E likewise applies to requests for **unlisted orthotics and prosthetics for adults** and requires that “the device being requested must fit the definition of an orthotic or prosthetic.” [unverified quote — not found in retrieved sources] [Policy 5B Attachment E](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/5b-orthotics-prosthetics/download?attachment)

Because chiropractic treatment is not an orthotic or prosthetic device under Policy 5B, it does not fit this policy’s covered service scope. [Policy 5B § 3.2.1](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/5b-orthotics-prosthetics/download?attachment) [Policy 5B Attachment E](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/5b-orthotics-prosthetics/download?attachment)

Policy 5B also says Medicaid does not cover a procedure, product, or service related to this policy when the beneficiary does not meet the criteria in Section 3.0. [Policy 5B § 4.1](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/5b-orthotics-prosthetics/download?attachment)

If the patient is **under 21**, Policy 5B includes an EPSDT special provision stating that medically necessary services may be covered beyond ordinary policy limits if they meet EPSDT criteria, but the section does not say that chiropractic treatment is itself covered under Policy 5B. [Policy 5B § 2.2.1](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/5b-orthotics-prosthetics/download?attachment)

If you want, I can also check whether **any other NC Medicaid policy** covers chiropractic treatment, separate from Policy 5B.

scores.explanation: The agent correctly answers 'No' and accurately explains that Policy 5B covers orthotic and prosthetic devices, not chiropractic treatment. The agent cites specific sections (3.2.1, 4.1, 2.2.1, Attachment E) that are all present in the evidence. The definitions of orthotic and prosthetic devices cited match the evidence from section 3.2.1. The agent flags one quote from Attachment E as '[unverified quote — not found in retrieved sources]', which is honest disclosure rather than hallucination. However, the actual Attachment E content in the evidence does contain the phrase 'The device being requested must fit the definition of an orthotic or prosthetic,' so the flagged quote is actually supported by evidence — the agent was overly cautious. The agent also correctly notes that chiropractic coverage would fall under a different policy, consistent with the reference answer. The answer is thorough, well-cited, and a Medicaid policy expert would find it acceptable and accurate.

uncited_claims: Policy 5B covers **orthotics and prosthetics** and related supplies or unlisted **devices** that fit the policy’s definition of an orthotic or prosthetic, not chiropractic treatment.

ID: sec:doc:clinical_policy:5B:Attachment E
Title: Attachment E: Requesting Unlisted Orthotics and Prosthetics for Adults
Section: Attachment E
Policy: 5B
Type: clinical_policy
Citation link: [Orthotics & Prosthetics](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/5b-orthotics-prosthetics/download?attachment)
Reason: Matched cover.
Content:
In compliance with the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services (CMS) Home Health Final Rule, 42 CFR Part 440.70, please follow these guidelines when requesting medical necessity reviews for Orthotics and Prosthetics for adults not listed in Attachment B or the O&P fee schedule.
The general requirements and criteria set forth in clinical coverage policy 5B must be met. This includes, but is not limited to:
The device being requested must fit the definition of an orthotic or prosthetic;
The beneficiary must be enrolled in the NC Medicaid program and be eligible for the device;
The provider must be enrolled in the NC Medicaid program with an appropriate taxonomy;
The requested device must be safe, effective, economical and not intended for the convenience of the beneficiary, the beneficiary's caregiver, or the provider;
The device must be medical in nature, generally recognized as an accepted method of treatment, and must not be experimental or investigational;
The device must be ordered by a physician, physician assistant, or nurse practitioner;
The device must be medically necessary to maintain or improve a beneficiary's medical, physical or functional level, and appropriate for use in any non-institutional setting in which normal life activities take place;
A documented face-to-face encounter with the beneficiary and the ordering physician, physician assistant, or nurse practitioner related to the primary reason the beneficiary requires the device must have occurred no more than six months prior to the initiation of orthotics and prosthetics; and
The beneficiary's need for the device must be reviewed by the ordering physician, physician assistant, or nurse practitioner at least annually.
If the provider determines that the applicable requirements and criteria set forth in clinical coverage policy 5B have been met, then the provider may submit a completed Certificate of Medical Necessity/Prior Approval (CMN/PA) form and the usual supportive prior authorization documentation through NCTracks for a medical necessity review.
Providers may request non-covered, unlisted or restricted items using their identifiable HCPCS code. If no HCPCS code exists, providers may use the national miscellaneous code L8499 .
Items approved by this procedure may be manually priced. Please include the appropriate manual pricing documentation with the prior authorization request.
Providers should expect medical necessity reviews using this procedure to take longer than usual.
Claims for items approved using this procedure should also be submitted through NCTracks.
If denied, the provider and beneficiary will be notified, and normal beneficiary appeal rights will apply.
Providers will be notified if the device requested is covered by a different NC Medicaid policy area or waiver program.

Content:
Medicaid may place appropriate limits, based on medical necessity criteria, on Orthotics and Prosthetics. When the prescribing physician, physician assistant, or nurse practitioner, orders equipment or supplies beyond these limits, the provider shall seek prior authorization for these items through NCTracks.
A PA request for an override of a quantity limit, or lifetime expectancy must contain the usual PA documentation ( Subsections 5.2 and 5.3 ) along with the following additional information:
The item being requested for an override clearly marked on the CMN/PA form.
The type of override (quantity limit, or lifetime expectancy) clearly stated.
An explanation of the medical necessity for the override from the physician, physician assistant, nurse practitioner, or therapist.
Override PA requests are reviewed for medical necessity as per usual PA review timelines. Override PA review outcomes are communicated to providers and beneficiaries in the same way as a typical PA request.
Refer to Attachment B for a listing of the established lifetime expectancies and quantity limitations for Orthotics and Prosthetics. To request a medical necessity review for an item not listed, refer to sections 1.0 , 2.2 and Attachment E for instructions.

ID: sec:doc:clinical_policy:5B:3.2.1
Title: 3.2.1 Specific criteria covered by Medicaid
Section: 3.2.1
Policy: 5B
Type: clinical_policy
Citation link: [Orthotics & Prosthetics](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/5b-orthotics-prosthetics/download?attachment)
Reason: Matched limitation.
Content:
Medicaid shall cover orthotics and prosthetics when the beneficiary meets all the following specific criteria:
they are ordered by a physician, physician assistant, or nurse practitioner;
they are medically necessary to maintain or improve a beneficiary's medical, physical or functional level, and appropriate for use in any noninstitutional setting in which normal life activities take place;
a documented face-to-face encounter with the beneficiary and the ordering physician, physician assistant, or nurse practitioner related to the primary reason the beneficiary requires orthotics and prosthetics has occurred no more than six (6) months prior to the initiation of orthotics and prosthetics; and
the beneficiary's need for orthotics and prosthetics is reviewed by the ordering physician, physician assistant, or nurse practitioner at least annually.
Medicaid covers orthotic and prosthetic services when they are medically necessary, and the beneficiary meets the specific coverage requirements for the device.
Orthotic devices are medically necessary when required to correct or prevent skeletal deformities, to support or align movable body parts, or to preserve or improve physical function.
Prosthetic devices are medically necessary as a replacement for all or part of the function of a permanently inoperative, absent, or malfunctioning body part. The beneficiary shall require the prosthesis for mobility, daily care, or rehabilitation purposes.
In addition, orthotic and prosthetic devices must be:
a reasonable and medically necessary part of the beneficiary's treatment plan;
consistent with the beneficiary's diagnosis and medical condition, particularly the functional limitations and symptoms exhibited by the beneficiary; and
of high quality, with replacement parts available and obtainable.
Medical doctors (MDs), doctors of osteopathic medicine (DOs), doctors of podiatric medicine (DPMs), physician assistants (PAs) and nurse practitioners (NPs) may provide certain orthotic and prosthetic devices when the devices are part of the beneficiary's current care and treatment. These professionals may provide devices as indicated in the Required Provider Certification column of Attachment B .
To be reimbursed for an orthotic or prosthetic device, the provider shall be enrolled as an appropriate board-certified provider for the specific device. Refer to Attachment B, which includes the Required Professional Certification for Orthotic and Prosthetic Devices.
For specific coverage requirements, refer to Subsection 5.3, Documenting Medical Necessity.

Content:
42 U.S.C. § 1396d(r) [1905(r) of the Social Security Act]
Early and Periodic Screening, Diagnostic, and Treatment (EPSDT) is a federal Medicaid requirement that requires the state Medicaid agency to cover services, products, or procedures for Medicaid beneficiary under 21 years of age if the service is medically necessary health care to correct or ameliorate a defect, physical or mental illness, or a condition [health problem] identified through a screening examination (includes any evaluation by a physician or other licensed practitioner).
This means EPSDT covers most of the medical or remedial care a child needs to improve or maintain his or her health in the best condition possible, compensate for a health problem, prevent it from worsening, or prevent the development of additional health problems.
Medically necessary services will be provided in the most economic mode, as long as the treatment made available is similarly efficacious to the service requested by the beneficiary's physician, therapist, or other licensed practitioner; the determination process does not delay the delivery of the needed service; and the determination does not limit the beneficiary's right to a free choice of providers.
EPSDT does not require the state Medicaid agency to provide any service, product or procedure:
that is unsafe, ineffective, or experimental or investigational.
that is not medical in nature or not generally recognized as an accepted method of medical practice or treatment.
Service limitations on scope, amount, duration, frequency, location of service, and other specific criteria described in clinical coverage policies may be exceeded or may not apply as long as the provider's documentation shows that the requested service is medically necessary 'to correct or ameliorate a defect, physical or mental illness, or a condition' [health problem]; that is, provider documentation shows how the service, product, or procedure meets all EPSDT criteria, including to correct or improve or maintain the beneficiary's health in the best condition possible, compensate for a health problem, prevent it from worsening, or prevent the development of additional health problems.

per_question.question: If someone wants bariatric or body-contouring surgery purely for cosmetic weight-loss reasons with no medical necessity, does Policy 1A-15 (Surgery for Clinically Severe or Morbid Obesity) cover it?
per_question.agent_answer:
No. Policy 1A-15 covers bariatric surgery only when the beneficiary meets the policy’s specific medical criteria for clinically severe or morbid obesity; it does not cover surgery sought purely for cosmetic weight-loss reasons with no medical necessity. [Policy 1A-15 § 3.2.1](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/1a-15-surgery-clinically-severe-or-morbid-obesity/download?attachment)

The policy says Medicaid covers listed bariatric procedures only when health records substantiate that the beneficiary has met all required criteria, including a diagnosis of morbid obesity or clinically severe obesity with specified related conditions and documented unsuccessful non-surgical treatment. [Policy 1A-15 § 3.2.1](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/1a-15-surgery-clinically-severe-or-morbid-obesity/download?attachment)

For body-contouring or skin-removal surgery after weight loss, the policy expressly says that surgical removal of skin and fat folds “for solely cosmetic purposes is not covered.” [Policy 1A-15 § 4.2.1](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/1a-15-surgery-clinically-severe-or-morbid-obesity/download?attachment)

The same subsection directs readers to the reconstructive/cosmetic surgery policy for excessive skin removal criteria, which means coverage would depend on reconstructive criteria there, not on a purely cosmetic request under 1A-15. [Policy 1A-15 § 4.2.1](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/1a-15-surgery-clinically-severe-or-morbid-obesity/download?attachment)

Policy 1A-15 is currently effective October 1, 2024. [Policy 1A-15](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/1a-15-surgery-clinically-severe-or-morbid-obesity/download?attachment) The October 1, 2024 change notices identified in the amendment history affected Attachment A billing/table material, not the substantive cosmetic-exclusion language discussed above. [Policy 1A-15 Change Notice 2024-10-01](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/1a-15-surgery-clinically-severe-or-morbid-obesity/download?attachment) [Policy 1A-15 Change Notice 2024-10-01](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/1a-15-surgery-clinically-severe-or-morbid-obesity/download?attachment)

If you want, I can also check Policy 1-O-1 to see when post-bariatric body-contouring may qualify as reconstructive rather than cosmetic.

scores.explanation: The agent's answer is factually accurate and complete. It correctly states that Policy 1A-15 does not cover bariatric or body-contouring surgery for purely cosmetic purposes, citing the medical necessity criteria in 3.2.1 and the cosmetic exclusion in 4.2.1 (the agent calls it 4.2.1 which matches the evidence). The agent also correctly notes the cross-reference to Policy 1-O-1 for reconstructive criteria. Minor hallucination concern: the agent cites '§ 3.2.1' for the first claim about medical criteria (supported by evidence) and '§ 4.2.1' for the cosmetic exclusion (supported by evidence showing 'Cosmetic surgery...Surgical removal of this skin and fat for solely cosmetic purposes is not covered' in section 4.2.1). The reference answer mentions section 2.1.1 and 4.1 as the general exclusion, while the agent correctly points to 4.2.1 which is the specific cosmetic exclusion — this is actually more precise. The agent's claim that the October 2024 amendments 'affected Attachment A billing/table material, not the substantive cosmetic-exclusion language' is supported by the amendment evidence. Citation quality is good but uses hyperlinks rather than clean section references, and the agent incorrectly labels the cosmetic exclusion as '§ 4.2.1' in one place while the reference answer says section 4.1 — however the evidence clearly shows the cosmetic exclusion is in 4.2.1, making the agent more accurate than the reference on this point.

Content:
In addition to the specific criteria in Subsection 3.2.1 of this policy, Medicaid shall cover a surgical revision when the following is met:
Medicaid shall cover revision of a primary bariatric surgical procedure for a documented perioperative or late complication for a beneficiary who meets ONE of the below conditions:
weight loss of 20 percent or more below the ideal body weight;
esophagitis unresponsive to nonsurgical treatment;
hemorrhage or hematoma complicating a procedure;
excessive bilious vomiting following gastrointestinal surgery;
complications of the intestinal anastomosis and bypass;
stomal dilation, confirmed by endoscopy;
slippage of adjustable gastric band that cannot be corrected with manipulation or adjustments;
stricture;
obstruction;
erosion;
staple-line failure; or
non-absorption (such as hypoglycemia or malnutrition following gastrointestinal surgery).
Medicaid shall cover revision of a primary bariatric surgical procedure that has failed when pouch dilation is confirmed by upper gastrointestinal examination or endoscopy, producing weight gain of 20% or more, provided that:
the primary procedure was successful in inducing weight loss prior to the pouch dilation; and
the beneficiary has been compliant with a prescribed nutrition and exercise program following the procedure (weight and BMI prior to surgery, at lowest stable point, and at current time must be submitted along with surgeon's statement of compliance with diet and exercise).
